title: Junction Hook Errors in the Color Code
abstract: Color-dependent syndrome extraction schedules have been proposed to mitigate hook errors in the triangular color code. Recent work by Kishony and Fowler (arXiv:2603.28852) identifies distance-reducing hook errors by the type of anyon for which they provide a shortcut and chooses the CNOT ordering for stabilizers of each color to avoid these errors. We identify an additional class of distance-reducing hooks, which we call junction hook errors, that is not captured by this classification. The two data qubits of a junction hook error terminate anyon strings of two different colors at the point where the three colored strings of a logical operator meet, which we call the junction. As such, the hook error does not correspond to a single type of anyon, yet it still reduces the distance. For distances $d=7,9,11$, we verify that every non-corner plaquette admits a scheduled hook error that, together with $d-2$ single data qubit faults, produces an undetectable logical error using $d-1$ faults. Each of these is a junction hook error. Because of this, every stabilizer, including those in the bulk, still requires additional protection from hook errors (such as flag qubits) to restore the full circuit-level distance with this schedule. A minimum weight logical operator has at most one junction, however, so junction hook errors cannot accumulate on one minimum weight logical operator in the way that single-color malign hook errors can. This helps explain why the schedule still improves the circuit-level distance to $d-\lfloor (d+3)/6\rfloor$, rather than the $d/2$ distance associated with spatially uniform color code scheduling.
summary: This paper introduces 'junction hook errors,' a new type of correlated error in the triangular color code that reduces its effective distance. The authors demonstrate that these errors are not captured by prior analyses and necessitate strengthening the error correction protocol. This finding is crucial for building robust quantum computers based on topological codes.
main_problem: The paper identifies a novel class of distance-reducing errors in the triangular color code called 'junction hook errors,' which were missed by previous error classification schemes.
main_result: The existence of junction hook errors implies that the previously proposed syndrome extraction schedule is insufficient, requiring additional protection (like flag qubits) to restore the full circuit-level distance.
method: The authors analyze the structure of the color code, specifically examining how junction hook errors provide shortcuts for two different colored anyon strings meeting at a junction point.
model_or_system: The study uses the 2D triangular color code, a topological quantum error correction code, where logical operations are represented by colored string paths (red, green, blue) meeting at junctions.
key_observables: Circuit-level distance, undetectable logical errors, and the specific structure of junction hook errors occurring at junctions.
important_parameters: Code distance $d$, and specific values tested for $d$ include 7, 9, and 11.
main_assumptions: The analysis builds upon existing work on color-dependent syndrome extraction schedules but assumes the necessity of accounting for junction-specific errors.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate junction hook errors on the $d=9$ code, showing the meeting of three colored strings at a junction, and comparing the error location to minimum weight logical operators.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of junction hook errors, proves their existence by showing they cause undetectable logical errors for specific distances, and discusses the implications for maintaining the full circuit-level distance.
why_interesting: This work directly advances the theoretical understanding of fault-tolerance in topological quantum computing codes by identifying systematic weaknesses in existing error correction schedules.

The black dots form a minimum weight logical operator, which consists of a red, a green and a blue string. Each string begins on the boundary of its own color, and the three strings meet at the junction (dashed circle). The junction is a data qubit that does not belong to the logical operator but whose three neighbors do. These strings are all either perpendicular or “nearly” perpendicular to the boundary of the same color. Both are oriented perpendicular or nearly perpendicular to the boundary of the string’s color.
